title: Indians Posted to UK Now Avoid Double Social Security for Five Years
headline: Indians Posted to UK Now Avoid Double Social Security for Five Years
subheadline: The Double Contributions Convention, in force since July 15, extends the NIC exemption for detached workers from 52 weeks to 60 months — if they hold an EPFO Certificate of Coverage.
body:
• The India-UK Double Contributions Convention, in force since July 15, 2026, extends the social security exemption for detached workers from 52 weeks to 60 months.
  • Indian employees sent by an India-based employer to the UK for up to 60 months pay no UK National Insurance and keep contributing to India's EPF instead.
  • It does not apply if you move to the UK independently for a UK job, plan to stay over 60 months, or a family member takes UK work — NICs apply from day one in those cases.
  • Detached workers need a Certificate of Coverage from EPFO as proof; visa costs still apply, including a £769 application fee and £1,035 a year Immigration Health Surcharge for the Senior or Specialist Worker route cited by GOV.UK.

Indian employees posted to the United Kingdom by an India-based employer no longer face paying social security twice — once at home and once in Britain — for assignments of up to five years. The Double Contributions Convention (DCC) between India and the UK came into force on July 15, 2026, extending the exemption from 52 weeks to 60 months, according to Mint's explainer on the new EPF and NIC rules and the UK government.

The mechanism is simple, and it is not a waiver. A detached worker — an employee already working for an India-based employer who is sent temporarily to the UK — stops paying UK National Insurance contributions (NICs) and instead continues paying a similar amount into India's Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) scheme. The contribution record stays in one country instead of fragmenting across two.

What changed on July 15

Before the DCC, UK domestic rules exempted employees sent from a country without a relevant agreement for only the first 52 weeks. The DCC, agreed alongside the UK-India Comprehensive and Economic Trade Agreement (CETA), extends that period reciprocally to 60 months, the GOV.UK Double Contributions Convention explainer confirms. Mint reported the period was initially proposed at three years and was extended to five years when the agreement took effect.

https://x.com/Dr_Uditraj/status/2113504724427358546

The arrangement is reciprocal. UK employees sent to India for up to 60 months are exempt from India's EPF and keep paying UK NICs, building UK State Pension entitlement. Indian detached workers do not build UK State Pension entitlement during the assignment — they remain covered by India's system.

For UK staff in India, the underlying EPF exposure the DCC removes is substantial: Mint noted eligible International Workers generally face 12% employee and 12% employer contributions on basic wages and dearness allowance, a combined 24%.

Who qualifies — and who does not

The GOV.UK social security agreement guidance for the UK and India is precise about the boundary. Employees sent on or after July 15, 2026 remain subject to Indian legislation only if their UK work is not expected to exceed 60 months, and they should obtain a Certificate of Coverage from India's Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) as evidence.

Three groups fall outside it. Anyone who moves independently and takes a job with a UK employer pays NICs from the start. Anyone sent for a planned assignment exceeding 60 months pays NICs from the start. And a detached worker's family member who takes up employment in the UK must pay UK NICs under the normal rules. Workers already in the UK part-way through a 52-week exemption immediately before July 15, 2026 are also not detached workers under the DCC and became subject to UK legislation from that date, GOV.UK says.

"The Agreement on Social Security exempts Indian workers and employers from making dual social security contributions in the United Kingdom during temporary assignments."

— Ministry of Commerce and Industry, June 17, 2026 release, quoted by Mint

What the DCC does not change

The convention changes contributions only. It does not change immigration rules, visa eligibility or salary thresholds. GOV.UK's explainer cites the Senior or Specialist Worker route as an example: a minimum salary of £48,500 or the going rate for the role, whichever is higher, a visa application fee of £769, an Immigration Health Surcharge of £1,035 for up to 12 months and £1,035 for each additional year, plus an employer Immigration Skills Charge of £1,000 for the first year and £500 for each additional six months, and £525 for a Certificate of Sponsorship where applicable.

"If Indian workers and their employers cannot meet these requirements, they will not be given a visa, and they cannot benefit from the DCC," the UK government states. Article 8(7) also ensures Indian detached workers pay back into India's scheme on a similar basis while not paying NICs, so the DCC is not a discount on hiring — it is an end to paying twice.

For employers, the immediate task is paperwork: confirm the assignment will last no more than 60 months, and secure the EPFO Certificate of Coverage before payroll treats the posting as NIC-exempt.
